source: Grove et al. (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis
finding: Formula-based prediction beat clinical judgment on average, across tasks, judges and experience levels.
numbers: Mechanical about 10% more accurate on average. Mechanical substantially better in 33% to 47% of studies. Clinical substantially better in only 6% to 16%.
quote: mechanical-prediction techniques were about 10% more accurate than clinical predictions
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the full paper. A count of 136 studies came from a secondary note and is unchecked.
agent_relevance: S7 design is supported: model scores features, code combines. Do not let the model do the final weighing.

source: Grove et al. (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis (moderator: interview data)
finding: The clinician's disadvantage was larger when the predictors included a clinical interview.
numbers: Reported as a relative drop in clinical accuracy with interview data; no coefficient read.
limits: Abstract level only.
agent_relevance: Free-text impressions fed into a holistic verdict are the weakest input. Have the model score fixed features instead.

source: Grove et al. (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis (where clinical ties)
finding: Clinical judgment was often as good as the formula and rarely clearly better.
numbers: Clinical clearly better in 6% to 16% of studies; about equal in the rest.
limits: Abstract only. No systematic domain where the human won.
agent_relevance: Expect the model-as-judge to tie the formula sometimes and rarely beat it, so the cheap deterministic combiner is the safe default.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly, Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions: a meta-analysis
finding: Large replication in hiring and admissions: holistic combination lost validity, even for expert assessors who knew the jobs.
numbers: Job performance: validity .44 mechanical vs .28 clinical (over 50% better prediction). Advancement .42 vs .36. Training .31 vs .16. Grade point average .58 vs .48. Non-grade academic criteria .47 vs .46 (clinical side only 161 students).
quote: consistent and substantial loss of validity when data were combined holistically
limits: Under the strictest new-sample shrinkage the mechanical edge vanished but did not reverse for two criteria. Few studies for training and non-grade outcomes.
agent_relevance: Confirms Grove with a newer, narrower sample. The gap is smallest when the criterion is soft and data are few.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly, Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions: a meta-analysis (small N and weights)
finding: Authors answer the objections that formulas need big samples or exact weights.
numbers: Linear models stay strong unless weights flip sign; weights can come from the literature or pooled expert judgment (argument cites Dawes 1979).
limits: Argument, not a fresh experiment.
agent_relevance: The code combiner can use equal or expert-set weights. It does not need training data to beat holistic judgment.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: Top performers picked each year and put in elite teams stayed more accurate in later years; regression to the mean did not erase them.
numbers: Standardized Brier: superforecasters -0.34, top-team individuals -0.14, all others 0.04. AUC 96% vs 84% vs 75%. Resolution .40, .35, .32. 60 superforecasters in 5 teams of 12.
limits: Selection plus teaming plus environment cannot be fully separated. Geopolitical questions; volunteers mostly US men (83% men).
agent_relevance: Forecasting skill is real and stable. Consistency across attempts can be measured by code and used to weight samples.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions (learning rate)
finding: Superforecasters were better at the start and also improved faster as new information arrived.
numbers: Learning slope -0.26 for superforecasters vs -0.18 for top-team individuals vs 0 for all others (standardized Brier across a tournament year).
limits: Slopes from daily scores averaged over years 2 and 3.
agent_relevance: Updating on new evidence is a skill; schedule explicit update passes.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions (traits)
finding: Distinguishing traits: fluid intelligence, actively open-minded thinking, need for cognition, scope sensitivity.
numbers: Superforecasters at least 1 SD above the general population on fluid and on crystallized intelligence.
limits: Correlational. Traits cannot be copied into a model directly.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness maps to prompting for counter-arguments before scoring; test it as an operator.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions (granularity)
finding: Fine-grained probabilities carried information: rounding superforecasters' forecasts hurt their score.
numbers: Rounding to the nearest 0.10 hurt superforecasters but not the two comparison groups; accuracy was lost when going from 10 to 4 categories.
limits: Specific to the group that actually used fine distinctions.
agent_relevance: Do not round or bin model probabilities early; keep full precision until the final step.

source: Tetlock (2016) How much better can we get when we get serious about keeping score? (conference slides)
finding: Four-factor account of the tournament gains: identifying superforecasters, training, teaming, aggregation. Training targeted balancing inside and outside views.
numbers: Slide text: superforecaster teams saw about 400 days out as well as regular forecasters saw 150. A chart with shares of gain (roughly 10%, 10%, 25%) was garbled in extraction.
limits: Slides, not peer reviewed. Chart numbers unreliable.
agent_relevance: Aggregation and base-rate training look like the cheapest gains; both are code-checkable steps.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert Political Judgment (search summaries only)
finding: Founding result: about 284 experts forecast over about 20 years; barely better than chance and no better than simple statistical rules; foxes beat hedgehogs.
numbers: Search summaries gave 82,361 forecasts and 284 experts; not verified against the book.
limits: Book not opened (the link returned HTML). The 'dart-throwing chimp' wording was not confirmed in the sources seen.
agent_relevance: Experts are overconfident; this motivates forced probabilities scored by code.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, Mullainathan (2018) Human decisions and machine predictions
finding: A model trained on bail data beat judges when release decisions were re-ranked by predicted risk.
numbers: Same jailing rate: 24.7% fewer crimes. Same crime rate: 41.8% fewer people jailed. Riskiest 1% of defendants (predicted crime risk 62.6%): judges released 48.5% of them. 73.6% of defendants were released overall.
limits: Outcomes for people judges jailed are imputed, not observed. Quasi-random judge assignment. One US city system; observable features only.
agent_relevance: A modern field test of S7 logic: model predicts, rule decides. Also shows the selective-labels trap when evaluating any scoring model.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, Mullainathan (2018) Human decisions and machine predictions (mis-ranking)
finding: Detaining in order of predicted risk would do the same crime reduction with far fewer people jailed.
numbers: Jail only 48.2% as many people, or get a 75.8% larger crime reduction (32.9% vs 18.7% at a 13.0 point rise in jailing).
limits: Authors' counterfactual simulation.
agent_relevance: Support for removing free-form judgment from the last step.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval, fine-tuned reasoning and a trimmed-mean ensemble approach the human crowd on 914 held-out questions from 5 platforms.
numbers: Brier: system .179, human crowd .149, best zero-shot GPT-4-1106 .208, unskilled .25. Averaging system and crowd (4x crowd weight): .146 vs crowd .149.
limits: Test questions after June 2023. Later leakage critique applies (see Pitfalls entries).
agent_relevance: LLM judgment helps most as a complement to a stronger signal, combined by code.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models (ablations)
finding: Fine-tuning and retrieval each helped; the prompt alone gave little.
numbers: Full .179; no fine-tune .186; neither retrieval nor fine-tune .206 (near the .208 baseline); fine-tuned GPT-3.5 .182. Fine-tune set 13,253 samples.
limits: Fine-tuning needs training; our agent does not train, so retrieval and aggregation are the usable parts.
agent_relevance: Without training, expect scaffold gains from retrieval, decomposed queries and aggregation, not from prompt wording.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models (when it beats the crowd)
finding: System nears the crowd when at least 5 relevant articles are retrieved, and beats it when three conditions hold jointly (crowd uncertain, early retrieval, 5+ articles).
numbers: When the crowd forecast is between .3 and .7 the crowd Brier is .24. Jointly met, the system beats the crowd by more than 1.5 standard errors.
limits: Table cells were garbled in text extraction, so exact per-row Brier values are not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Report how much evidence was found and widen or abstain when evidence is thin.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
finding: Median of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd of 925 forecasters on 31 binary questions.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier .20 (SD .12) vs human crowd .19 (SD .19), t(60)=0.19, p=.850; vs .25 no-information, p=.026. Equivalence within d=0.5 (0.081 Brier) significant (exploratory).
limits: Only 31 questions from one three-month Metaculus tournament. Equivalence test not preregistered. Single models: GPT-4 .15, Claude 2 .21, Coral (Command) .38.
agent_relevance: Aggregate several model samples with code; a single run is noisy.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy (acquiescence)
finding: Models leaned toward yes: mean predictions were significantly above 50% though resolutions were nearly evenly split.
numbers: Significance reported; the human crowd mean was also above 50% (57.35%, SD 20.93).
limits: This question set only.
agent_relevance: Pair each question with its negation and check agreement by code.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy (Study 2: seeing the human median)
finding: GPT-4 and Claude 2 improved when shown the human crowd median, but a plain average of human and machine beat the model's own update.
numbers: Accuracy gain 17% to 28% after seeing the median.
limits: Two models; small sample.
agent_relevance: Averaging in code beats asking the model to integrate a crowd signal.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: On 200 questions, superforecasters beat both the public and the best LLM.
numbers: Brier: superforecasters .096, public .121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122 (p<.001). Best LLM without the crowd forecast: .136. With combination questions: superforecasters .076 vs GPT-4o .130.
limits: Top LLMs were given the market price as a 'freeze value'. 200-question human subsample. Combination items assume independence for humans, which understates them.
agent_relevance: Most machine gain came from a given strong prior; supply the agent with base rates and reference values.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (gap sizes)
finding: The superforecaster-to-GPT-4o gap was larger than the GPT-4o-to-GPT-4 gap.
numbers: Gap superforecasters vs GPT-4o 0.054, larger than the 0.026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Combination-question benchmark.
agent_relevance: Scale alone closes the gap slowly; scaffolding is the other lever.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2025) How well can large language models predict the future? (ForecastBench update, blog)
finding: By October 2025 the best LLM trailed superforecasters by a modest margin, and the median public forecast fell behind many LLMs.
numbers: GPT-4.5 .101 vs superforecasters .081 (difficulty-adjusted). GPT-4 .131. About 0.016 Brier improvement per year. Public median rank 2 to 22 in a year. Parity projected November 2026, 95% CI Dec 2025 to Jan 2028.
limits: GPT-4.5 correlated .994 with supplied market prices and copied exact values on 26 of 122 questions. Linear extrapolation. Basic prompts, no news. Binary only.
agent_relevance: Market-question scores overstate skill; the agent must not claim skill where it can copy the crowd.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) LLMs are closing the gap on human superforecasters (blog)
finding: January 2026: superforecasters still first; gap 0.017 Brier, about one year of LLM progress.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) .117; Grok 4.20 preview .102; an ensemble with crowd adjustment beat its plain ensemble by nearly 0.01. Parity projection Nov 2026, CI Jan 2026 to Nov 2027.
limits: No question overlap between the first superforecaster sample and the latest models. Preview model. Secondary web reports (not opened) say AI still trailed in mid-2026 and the metric changed to a Brier Index in March 2026.
agent_relevance: Crowd adjustment as a code step gives a measurable gain.

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic forecasting using sequential Bayesian updating of linguistic beliefs
finding: An agentic forecaster with a belief state, sequential search, 5-trial logit averaging and calibration matched the superforecaster median in backtest.
numbers: Brier Index (higher is better): 73.8 vs best external 70.8. Superforecaster median 70.9, this system 71.0 (different question sets). Ablations: zero-shot -5.6; no search -4.6; batch search -3.8; no belief state -3.0; crowd signal +3.7; leaked future +9.5.
limits: Backtest, 400 questions, 791 resolution dates, mostly one base model. Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read. Residual leakage 1.5%.
agent_relevance: Direct support for sequential search plus a belief state held by code plus code aggregation. Most of the gain needs no training.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Logical consistency of a forecaster's probabilities (arbitrage metric) tracks its later Brier score for some checks.
numbers: Some checks (conditional probabilities) correlate above R=0.9 with Brier score; others give little signal. 10 check types; a 3,000-check benchmark resolving in 2028.
limits: Few forecasters; correlational.
agent_relevance: Code can run cheap consistency checks (negation, and-or) as a label-free quality signal for S7 outputs.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters (patching)
finding: A forecaster patched to be consistent on trained checks did not improve on held-out checks or in accuracy.
numbers: ArbitrageForecaster improved the targeted consistency only; no Brier gain.
limits: Authors' own setup.
agent_relevance: Use consistency to detect problems, not to fix them.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters
finding: Many LLM forecasting claims may be inflated by temporal leakage and weak benchmark design.
numbers: At least 3.8% of one dataset and at least 10% of another were leaking or trivial; weak classifiers reach above 80% on one news-generated set; over 90% of one set judged over-specific; 1 to 5% resolution error with Perplexity-based retrieval.
limits: Position paper; some judgments are subjective by the authors' own admission.
agent_relevance: Treat reported LLM parity claims as upper bounds; our tests must use live or post-cutoff questions.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters (Brier base-rate trap)
finding: Average Brier is not comparable across base rates, so a mix of easy rare-event questions can mislead.
numbers: Example: 50 coin-flip plus 50 rare (5%) questions. Perfect on the rare ones gives about 0.125 total; improving the coin-flip ones from .25 to .15 gives about 0.10 and looks better.
limits: Constructed illustration.
agent_relevance: Report Brier with calibration and base-rate-adjusted scores, never raw Brier alone.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: 991 participants answering six questions did better with a frontier LLM assistant, even one told to be overconfident and ignore base rates.
numbers: Accuracy gain 24% to 28% vs control; excluding one outlier item, 41% for the good assistant and 29% for the noisy one. Preregistered.
limits: Control was a weaker model, not no help. Effect depends on one outlier item. Hypotheses on diversity and low-skill benefit not supported.
agent_relevance: Even a noisy LLM adviser helps humans; for an agent this suggests generating many views and letting code filter.
